explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul says men ought to regard him and Apollos, another teacher, as “…servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God.” Notice what's missing: no throne, no trophy, no team jersey. A servant works for somebody else, and Paul wants that to be the picture.

Close to the opposite, friend. Paul says servants, and a master is the one a servant answers to. It's a big title for a man who just called himself a servant of Christ. Nowhere in this verse does he ask the Corinthians to see him or Apollos, another teacher, as masters.

Not this time, baker. Paul says servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God, and no judge's robe shows up in the verse. A few verses later he says it's the Lord who judges him (1 Corinthians 4:4). And he tells the Corinthians to judge nothing before the appointed time (1 Corinthians 4:5). Nobody in this passage is picking up the gavel.

Faithful, baker. Paul says, “Now it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.” Look at what he asks for. He doesn't ask for talent or a big following, just faithful. I like that, because anybody can do faithful, even a worn-out stamper.

Famous is a fun guess, friend, but it's not in the verse. Paul says stewards must be found faithful. Fame is exactly what you'd chase if you were picking a favorite teacher, and Paul doesn't ask for it. Nobody puts "most famous" on a cookie box, and nobody in this verse asks for it either.

Clever sounds right, baker, but that's not what Paul says. The verse says it is required of stewards that they be found faithful. Being clever might get you a few compliments, but it's not the requirement here. Showing up and being trusted is.

True, baker. Paul says, “In fact, I do not even judge myself.” He's already said he cares very little about being judged by the Corinthians or by any human court. So he's not holding a clipboard over himself either. I can barely take a bite of my own cookies without grading the corners.

The verse says the opposite, friend. Paul says, “In fact, I do not even judge myself.” That comes right after he says he cares very little if he's judged by the Corinthians or by any human court (1 Corinthians 4:3). So it's True, and no judging from himself either.
Yes, baker. Paul says, “My conscience is clear, but that does not vindicate me. It is the Lord who judges me.” So even a clear conscience doesn't get the final say. The Lord does.

Not the apostles, friend. Paul is one himself, and he says it's the Lord who judges him. His clear conscience doesn't vindicate him, and a vote from his fellow apostles isn't mentioned either. The verse puts the judging in the Lord's hands.

Elders don't show up in this verse, baker. Paul says, “It is the Lord who judges me.” He's already said he cares very little about a human court (1 Corinthians 4:3). So a panel of elders isn't the answer. The Lord is.

That's it, baker. Paul says the Lord “…will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and will expose the motives of men’s hearts.” So it's not only what people did, but why. Which is a good reason to hold off on judging, since we only see part of it.

Nations aren't in this verse, friend. Paul says the Lord will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and will expose the motives of men’s hearts. The focus is on the hearts of people. That's why he says to judge nothing before the appointed time.

No false prophets here, baker. Paul says the Lord will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and will expose “…the motives of men’s hearts.” He doesn't single out any one group. He's talking about everybody's motives, and that includes the Corinthians' own.
Close, but the praise comes from somewhere else, friend. Paul says, “At that time each will receive his praise from God.” Not from the church, and not from a fan club. That's a much better source.
False is right, baker. Paul says, “At that time each will receive his praise from God.” It doesn't come from the church. Nobody has to campaign for votes in that moment.

explanations.answer: Not to go beyond what is written
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Paul says he applied these things to himself and Apollos so “…that you may learn from us not to go beyond what is written.” Then, he says, they won't take pride in one man over another. Sounds like a good reason to keep our noses in the Book.

explanations.answer: Not to seek after signs and wonders
explanations.explanation: That one isn't in the verse, friend. Paul says the lesson is “…not to go beyond what is written.” Signs and wonders don't come up here. The point is to stay with what's written.

explanations.answer: Not to turn away from the elders
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. Elders aren't mentioned in this verse. Paul says the Corinthians should learn from him and Apollos “…not to go beyond what is written.” After that, he says, they won't take pride in one man over another.

Pride, baker. Paul says, “Then you will not take pride in one man over another.” That's the fan club problem in one sentence. Learn not to go beyond what is written, and nobody needs to brag about their favorite teacher.

Refuge sounds nice, friend, but that's not the word. Paul says they won't take pride in one man over another. He's talking about boasting over favorites, not finding shelter. Nobody in this verse is running for cover.
Comfort doesn't fit here, baker. Paul says, “Then you will not take pride in one man over another.” The trouble in Corinth was bragging about which teacher they followed. So the word is pride.

explanations.answer: Everything they have was given to them
explanations.explanation: That's his point, baker. Paul asks, “What do you have that you did not receive?” If everything was received, then there's nothing to brag about. A gift is a gift.

explanations.answer: They should give away what they own
explanations.explanation: That's not what Paul is asking for, friend. He asks, “What do you have that you did not receive?” He doesn't tell them to give anything away. He's showing them that what they have was received, so there's no reason to boast.

explanations.answer: They have not worked hard enough
explanations.explanation: Paul never says that, baker. His question is, “What do you have that you did not receive?” He's not measuring how hard they worked. His point is that they received what they have, so boasting makes no sense.
Other way around, friend. Paul asks, “And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?” So receiving it is exactly why boasting doesn't fit. It's False.

False is right, baker. Paul asks, “And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?” Once you see something was given to you, there's nothing left to brag about. I've learned to say "thank you" before "look at me."

That's the wish, baker. Paul says, “How I wish you really were kings, so that we might be kings with you!” They've already crowned themselves, he says. And if it were true, he'd get to share it with them.

explanations.answer: That they would give up their crowns
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Paul says he wishes they really were kings, “…so that we might be kings with you!” He doesn't ask them to hand anything back. He's wishing it were true.

explanations.answer: That they would share their riches
explanations.explanation: That's not his wish, baker. Paul says, “How I wish you really were kings, so that we might be kings with you!” Sharing riches isn't mentioned. He's wishing they really were kings.
Bigger than that, baker. Paul says the apostles have become “…a spectacle to the whole world, to angels as well as to men.” That's more than men. It's False.
False is right, friend. Paul says the apostles have become “…a spectacle to the whole world, to angels as well as to men.” So the audience isn't just men. Angels are watching too.
Strong, baker. Paul says, “We are weak, but you are strong.” He's lining the apostles up next to the Corinthians, and that's how the comparison goes. It's a hard line to read, but that's the word.
Humble is a good word, friend, but it isn't Paul's here. He says, “We are weak, but you are strong.” The line sets the apostles against the Corinthians, and the Corinthians get the strong side.

Gentle shows up later, baker, but not in this line. Paul says, “We are weak, but you are strong.” Gentle is how the apostles answer when they're slandered (1 Corinthians 4:13). Here the word is strong.
That's it, baker. Paul says, “When we are vilified, we bless.” When somebody insults you, blessing them back is a tough move. I think I would've needed a minute in the pantry first.
Opposite, friend. Paul says, “When we are vilified, we bless.” The apostles don't hit back with insults. They bless.

Leaving town isn't in this verse, baker. Paul says, “When we are vilified, we bless; when we are persecuted, we endure it.” They bless when insulted, and they endure when persecuted. So the answer is bless.
True, baker. Paul says, “…when we are slandered, we answer gently.” Somebody spreads a lie about you, and you answer gently. That takes a lot of strength.
The text says the opposite, friend. Paul says, “…when we are slandered, we answer gently.” So it's True. They don't snap back.

explanations.answer: To warn them as his beloved children
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Paul says, “I am not writing this to shame you, but to warn you as my beloved children.” It's a warning, and it comes with love. He's talking like a father.

explanations.answer: To shame them in front of others
explanations.explanation: Paul says the opposite, friend. He writes, “I am not writing this to shame you, but to warn you as my beloved children.” So shame is exactly what he says he isn't doing. A warning from a father is a different thing.

explanations.answer: To prove he is the better teacher
explanations.explanation: That isn't what he says, baker. Paul writes, “I am not writing this to shame you, but to warn you as my beloved children.” He doesn't say anything about being the better teacher. He says he's warning them.

Imitate, baker. Paul says, “Therefore I urge you to imitate me.” He's just told them he became their father in Christ Jesus through the gospel (1 Corinthians 4:15). So he asks them to follow his example.
Defend isn't the word, friend. Paul says, “Therefore I urge you to imitate me.” He's not asking for a defense. He's asking them to follow his example.
Thank is a nice thought, baker, but it's not what Paul asks. He says, “Therefore I urge you to imitate me.” The request is to follow his example, not to give him a thank-you.

explanations.answer: Remind them of Paul's way of life
explanations.explanation: That's the job, baker. Paul says Timothy “…will remind you of my way of life in Christ Jesus, which is exactly what I teach everywhere in every church.” So Timothy brings a reminder of how Paul lives. It matches what Paul teaches everywhere.

explanations.answer: Choose new leaders for their church
explanations.explanation: Nothing about new leaders, friend. Paul says Timothy “…will remind you of my way of life in Christ Jesus…” His job is to remind them of Paul's way of life.

explanations.answer: Collect a gift to bring back to Paul
explanations.explanation: No gift in this verse, baker. Paul says Timothy will remind the Corinthians of his way of life in Christ Jesus. A collection isn't mentioned. The job is a reminder.
True, baker. Paul says, “But I will come to you shortly, if the Lord is willing.” He's sending Timothy, and he's coming himself too. Some of them figured he wouldn't show up (1 Corinthians 4:18).
The verse says otherwise, friend. Paul says, “But I will come to you shortly, if the Lord is willing.” So it's True. He plans to show up.
That's it, baker. Paul says he will find out “…not only what these arrogant people are saying, but what power they have.” Talking is easy. He wants to see what's behind it.

Money isn't in this verse, friend. Paul says he will find out “…not only what these arrogant people are saying, but what power they have.” Power is what he's after. The Corinthians' bank accounts don't come up.

Not that one, baker. Paul says he'll find out “…not only what these arrogant people are saying, but what power they have.” Who taught them first isn't in the verse. The thing he wants to see is their power.
Opposite, friend. Paul says, “For the kingdom of God is not a matter of talk but of power.” So it's False. Talk alone doesn't cut it.

False, baker. Paul says, “For the kingdom of God is not a matter of talk but of power.” That fits what he just said about finding out what power the arrogant people have. Plenty of folks can talk. Power is what he wants to see.
